reviewer: Pickle: official-source winter static electricity, knit charge, anti-static spray, dryer wool balls and discharge comparison guide
method: Reviewed the draft against 24 sources on 2026-11-11. Charge values: Anritsu 2024 ESD basics sheet (direct PDF read) gives taking off an acrylic sweater 4,500–5,000 V, polyester work clothes 4,000–4,500 V, standing up from a sofa 3,500–4,500 V, folding an acrylic blanket 5,000–6,000 V at 25 °C/40 %RH, and a sensation table of 1,000 V (not felt), 2,000 V (foreign body), 2,500 V (needle, no pain), 3,000 V (needle, slight pain), 4,000 V (deep needle pain). Humidity: NASA EEE Parts ESD Compendium Table 2 (citing MIL-HDBK-263B) 35,000 V at 10–20 %RH versus 1,500 V at 65–90 %RH for walking on carpet; KSC GSE-3008 gives 35,000/15,000/7,500 V at 10/40/50 %RH, states ESD is not normally a concern above 50 %RH and recommends 40–60 %RH; Maxim App Note 4491 gives 5,000 V jumping about 1 cm at 50 %RH; 행정안전부 안전한TV repeats 35,000 V versus 220 V household supply. Korean indoor measurements: KIEAE 2013 Cheongju field study of 20 apartments, winter RH 23.0–54.1 % (mean 35.4 %), 6 units below the 50±20 % criterion with a mean of 26.7 %, and the paper describes sub-30 % indoor air as markedly dry. KDCA winter health guidance sets 40–50 % indoor humidity; 환경부 실내공기질 guidance sets 18–22 °C and 40–60 %. Fabric softener: KCA 2017 comparison of 11 liquid softeners — anti-static performance good on cotton and wool for every product but insufficient on 100 % polyester for every product, with an explicit warning that overdosing reduces absorbency and leaves a sticky feel. Anti-static sprays: Lion エレガード FAQ states the spray must go on worn clothing, spraying a door does nothing, the effect lasts until the next wash or dry clean and fades with wear, acrylic/polyester charge negative while nylon/wool charge positive, and static attracts pollen and PM2.5. The 表面技術協会 review describes coating-type antistatic agents built on cationic surfactants (with nonionic wetting agents) whose conductivity appears only by adsorbing atmospheric moisture, so performance depends on humidity. 松岡 1980 measured larger charge density for knitted goods than woven fabrics when taking clothes off and named humidity control as the most effective countermeasure. Wool: Woolmark and IWTO both state wool absorbs up to 35 % of its own weight in moisture vapour. Dryer balls: CHOICE (2024-03-07) measured no meaningful energy or time difference in a vented and a condenser dryer (Wooly Mates 6 balls +0.15 kWh / −0.07 kWh); Prudent Reviews (2018) ran five control and five ball loads, 47 min 37 s down to 41 min 20 s (14 %), with static cling 4 versus 3 instances and an explicit inconclusive verdict; Expert Reviews (2025) saw a five-minute towel improvement and softer fabrics. Dust: Li et al. 2023 (Zhengzhou) exposed polyester, polyester-cotton and cotton clothing to PM2.5 for 1, 2 and 3 h and found polyester released the highest indoor PM2.5. Discharge: 전기신문 (2025-02-07, KERI material) reports a 35,000 V maximum with 0.00002 s duration and recommends touching a coin or metal object first; McGill OSS names humidity as the single biggest factor. Safety pin: Galaxus (2022-11-10) found a pinned garment did not lose its charge and rated the pin ineffective even as prevention, while its anti-static spray test reduced static noticeably; Snuggle lists the pocket safety pin as a myth and names over-drying as a cause. I deliberately did NOT use the widely circulated '3x more dust and bacteria' figure: no official test or paper supports a 3x multiplier for dust or bacteria adhesion, and the draft states that explicitly instead of repeating it; the claim that static electricity damages fibres directly was likewise dropped for lack of a source.
